column4: The system shall let an analyst compare conversion rates across fitting rooms and store locations.

column10: As a retail analyst, I want to compare conversion rates across fitting rooms and store locations so that I can identify performance outliers.

column4: The system shall track and display average dwell time per item and per fitting room.
column7: Alert Technologies benchmark: deviations from the 5m 45s average signal engagement or comfort issues in specific rooms or with specific items.
column8: Average dwell time per item and per room is available within 24 hours of data collection; values deviating from the 5m45s benchmark are visually flagged.
column10: As a retail analyst, I want to track average time spent per item in the fitting room so that I can benchmark against the 5m 45s industry average.

column4: The system shall let a retail manager export fitting-room reports as CSV or PDF.
column7: RW&Co interview: a monthly form is submitted to HQ requesting specific feedback, a structured export replaces this manual process.
column8: An export completes within 10 seconds and includes all currently visible filters and the selected date range.
column10: As a retail manager, I want to export fitting-room reports as CSV or PDF so that I can share insights with corporate buyers.

column4: Session data shall be collected and stored without any personally identifiable information.
column7: Privacy concerns are cited as a top barrier to sharing personal information in-store; 74% of consumers are willing if data use is transparent.
column8: No PII fields are present in the session data schema; records are keyed only by fitting-room ID and timestamp.
column10: As a shopper, I want my fitting-room session data collected anonymously so that I feel safe using the system.

column4: The tablet interface shall become fully interactive within 3 seconds on a standard store network connection.
column7: Oak Labs' 90% engagement rate depended on seamless in-room technology; slow load times would immediately deter use.
column8: The tablet UI is fully interactive within 3 seconds on a 10 Mbps connection, confirmed across repeated test runs.
column10: As a retailer, I want the tablet interface to load within 3 seconds on a standard store Wi-Fi connection so that shoppers are not left waiting.

column4: The system shall integrate with existing retailer POS systems without requiring custom hardware beyond a tablet and a standard barcode scanner.
column7: Oak Labs' failure case shows expensive custom hardware (RFID + smart mirrors) prevented scaling; keeping hardware minimal is essential.
column8: The system successfully reconciles POS transactions with fitting-room sessions using existing retailer POS infrastructure without requiring additional hardware beyond a tablet and barcode scanner.
column10: As a retailer, I want the system to integrate with my existing POS without custom hardware beyond a tablet so that implementation cost stays low.

column4: The tablet UI shall conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA accessibility standards.
column7: Shopper form shows 'ease of use and intuitiveness' is the top-cited interface attribute; accessibility underpins usable design.
column8: All interactive elements are reachable by keyboard and touch, and colour contrast meets a minimum ratio of 4.5:1.
column10: As a retailer, I want the tablet UI to meet WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standards so that all shoppers can use it independently.

column4: The system shall store and process data in compliance with PIPEDA and GDPR.
column7: Data privacy is a named concern in shopper research; retailers will require compliance guarantees before adoption.
column8: Documented data residency, retention, and deletion practices pass a compliance checklist aligned to PIPEDA and GDPR.
column10: As a retailer, I want all system data stored and processed in compliance with PIPEDA/GDPR so that I have no legal exposure.

column4: The system shall support scaling from a single-room pilot to a full multi-room rollout.
column7: Under Armour's connected fitting-room pilot model demonstrates that incremental rollout is the standard adoption path for in-store tech.
column8: The system operates correctly with both single-room and multi-room deployments using the same application build and configuration.
column10: As a retailer, I want the system to support a pilot deployment of 1-5 fitting rooms before a full rollout so that adoption risk stays low.

column4: The system shall preserve session data through brief interruptions in store network connectivity.
column7: Physical store environments have unreliable connectivity; data loss during a session would erode retailer trust in the system.
column8: No session data is lost during a simulated network interruption of up to 10 minutes; all data is present after reconnection.
column10: As a retailer, I want the system to function if the store Wi-Fi drops briefly so that a network interruption does not lose session data.
